title: Test Your Understanding: Idempotency and Delivery Guarantees
description: Idempotency keys, delivery guarantees, outbox pattern, and duplicate-handling trade-offs — not just definitions.

questions.question: Which operation is naturally idempotent?

options.text: `POST /orders` creating a new order each time

questions.explanation: Setting status to a fixed value yields the same end state if run twice. Inserts, unconditional decrements, and send-email side effects accumulate with each run.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of an idempotency key on a payment API?

options.text: To identify a logical operation so retries return the same result without repeating the charge

questions.explanation: The client sends one key per user intent (e.g. checkout). The server stores the result; duplicate requests with the same key replay the stored response instead of charging again.

questions.question: At-least-once message delivery means:

options.text: Messages may be lost but never duplicated
Messages are delivered one or more times; consumers may see duplicates
Messages are processed exactly once without any application logic

questions.explanation: At-least-once avoids loss by redelivering when ack fails or consumers crash mid-processing. Duplicates are expected — idempotent consumers or dedup tables handle them.

questions.question: What does "exactly-once-ish" processing usually mean in production?

options.text: At-least-once delivery plus idempotent consumers or dedup so side effects happen once

questions.explanation: True exactly-once end-to-end is hard and expensive. Most teams accept at-least-once transport and ensure at-most-once effects via idempotency keys, dedup tables, or conditional writes.

questions.question: What problem does the transactional outbox pattern solve?

options.text: Dual-write inconsistency between DB commit and message publish
Hot keys on a consistent hash ring

questions.explanation: The outbox writes business data and an outbox event row in one DB transaction. A relay publishes from the outbox — avoiding 'DB succeeded, publish failed' (or the reverse) from uncoordinated dual writes.

questions.question: A client retries `POST /charge` with a NEW idempotency key on each attempt. What is the likely outcome?

options.text: Only one charge — keys are optional
Multiple charges — each attempt looks like a new operation

questions.explanation: Idempotency keys must be stable per logical operation. A new key per retry defeats dedup — the server treats each as a distinct charge.

questions.question: Why should idempotency record inserts use a unique constraint (or equivalent)?

options.text: To prevent two concurrent requests with the same key both executing the side effect
To guarantee FIFO queue ordering globally

questions.explanation: Check-then-act races let two parallel requests both pass 'key not found' and double-charge. Atomic insert-with-conflict (or lock) ensures only one executes the side effect.

questions.question: Webhook handlers should deduplicate by provider event ID because providers often retry delivery on non-2xx responses.
questions.explanation: Stripe, GitHub, and others redeliver until you return success. The same event ID may arrive multiple times — store processed IDs and skip duplicates.
